title: Methodology & Glossary
body:
This page explains how the ratings, badges, and tiers you see across the Models and Tracker pages are worked out, and defines the technical terms we use so you don't need to look them up elsewhere.

### How we assess models

Every rating on this site is compiled through monthly research — reading each model's own documentation, current independent benchmarks, and recent hands-on reporting — then converted into the plain-English labels you see, with a human review before anything goes live. It's an editorial judgment call informed by that research, not a single automated score piped in from one provider — AI capability doesn't reduce to one number, and we'd rather be upfront about that than dress up a synthesis as more mechanical than it is.

We re-check the site every month and correct anything that's fallen out of date. If you think something's wrong, [contact us](/) — corrections to existing pages are always welcome.

### Status badges (Models page)

The badge in the top corner of each card — Market Leader, Highly Competitive, and so on — is a snapshot of where that model family sits relative to the rest of the field *right now*, based on how it performs in independent benchmarks and hands-on comparisons, how it's priced relative to comparable models, and how recently it's been meaningfully updated. It's a relative ranking, not an absolute score — a model can be genuinely excellent and still not carry the top badge if a competitor is ahead on more of those measures this month.

- **Market Leader** — currently the most-used and most-referenced model in its category, typically the default most people reach for first.
- **Highly Competitive** — matches or beats the leader on capability in most head-to-head comparisons, without the same scale of adoption.
- **Rising** — improving quickly release over release, and closing the gap on the leaders faster than the field average.
- **Disruptor** — changes the competitive picture by being dramatically cheaper, more open, or more specialized than the leaders, rather than by being the strongest all-rounder.

These labels are re-evaluated every time a card is refreshed, so they can and do change month to month as models are updated.

### Tracker scores: Speed, Reasoning, Cost

The three bars on each Tracker entry are a beginner-friendly translation of published benchmark results and pricing, checked each month against current sources — not a lab-run test we perform ourselves.

- **Speed** — how quickly the model responds in typical use, based on published latency/throughput figures and hands-on reports. Higher scores mean faster responses, which matters more for chat and less for long research tasks.
- **Reasoning** — performance on independent multi-step reasoning, math, and coding benchmarks (the kind of tasks where a model has to work through a problem rather than recall a fact).
- **Cost** — priced relative to the rest of the current field, not in absolute dollars. A higher Cost score means cheaper, not better — a free or open-weight model can score 90%+ here even if its Reasoning score is more modest.

These three scores are independent of each other on purpose: a model can be fast and cheap without being the strongest reasoner, and that trade-off is usually the most useful thing to know before picking one.

### Cost Tier

The label next to each model's Cost Tier is a rough guide to what you'd actually pay to use it, based on our most recent pricing review, grouped into five bands:

| Label | Blended price (USD per million tokens) | Example (as of this review) |
|---|---|---|
| **Free** | $0 for standard/consumer use (a paid tier may still exist for heavy or commercial use) | Gemini free tier, hosted open-weight demos |
| **Ultra-low** | roughly $0–$1 | GPT-4.1 nano, Gemini Flash-Lite |
| **Low** | roughly $1–$3 | Claude Haiku 4.5 |
| **Standard** | roughly $3–$8 | Claude Sonnet 5, Gemini 3.1 Pro |
| **Premium** | $8+ | Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5 |

Prices move often, so treat these bands as a snapshot, not a fixed rule. For exact current figures, check the provider's own pricing page.

### Glossary

**Closed API** — you can only use the model by sending requests to the maker's own servers (e.g. via ChatGPT or the OpenAI API). You never get the underlying model file, and the maker controls availability, pricing, and updates.

**Open weights** — the maker publishes the trained model file itself, so anyone can download it and run it on their own hardware (or a third-party host), inspect how it behaves, and fine-tune it. "Open weights" is not the same as "open source" — the training data and code used to build the model are usually still private, even when the weights are public.

**Frontier model** — one of the handful of models, from any maker, that currently represents the best publicly available capability. This is a moving target — today's frontier model is next year's mid-tier model.

**Context window** — how much text (measured in tokens) a model can "see" at once, including your prompt, any documents you've attached, and the conversation so far. A larger context window means it can work with longer documents or longer conversations without losing track of earlier parts.

**Token** — the basic unit a model reads and writes text in — roughly ¾ of a word in English on average. Pricing and context windows are almost always measured in tokens, not words or characters.

**Reasoning model** — a model specifically trained to work through problems step by step before answering, rather than responding immediately. This tends to improve accuracy on math, logic, and coding tasks, usually at the cost of a slower response.

**Mixture-of-Experts (MoE)** — an architecture where a model is built from many smaller specialized sub-networks ("experts"), and only a handful are activated for any given request. This lets a model have a very large total parameter count while keeping the cost of answering any one question much lower — part of why some very capable models are also comparatively cheap to run.

**Parameters** — the internal numerical values a model learns during training. Roughly speaking, more parameters mean more capacity to learn patterns, though modern smaller models trained well can outperform older larger ones — parameter count alone is a poor predictor of quality.

**Benchmark** — a standardized test used to compare models on a specific skill (e.g. coding, math, general knowledge). No single benchmark captures overall quality, which is why we weigh several rather than quoting one score.

**Fine-tuning** — additional training applied to an already-trained model to specialize it for a particular task, tone, or dataset, without starting from scratch.
